question: A session-store cache backed by ElastiCache for Redis must remain available with automatic failover if the primary node fails, and must support scaling read and write throughput horizontally beyond what a single node can provide by sharding data across multiple nodes.

options.A: Use ElastiCache for Redis with Cluster Mode enabled, configuring multiple shards, each with a primary and at least one read replica across different Availability Zones, with Multi-AZ automatic failover enabled so a replica is promoted automatically if a shard's primary fails.
options.B: Use ElastiCache for Memcached with multiple nodes, since Memcached natively supports both automatic failover and data sharding.
options.C: Use a single large ElastiCache for Redis node with Cluster Mode disabled and no replicas, and vertically scale it whenever more throughput is needed.
options.D: Use ElastiCache for Redis with Cluster Mode disabled, manually add read replicas without Multi-AZ, and perform manual failover via the console if the primary fails.

explanation: A session-store cache backed by ElastiCache for Redis must remain available with automatic failover if the primary node fails, and must support scaling read and write throughput horizontally beyond what a single node can provide by sharding data across multiple nodes. A. ✓ Use ElastiCache for Redis with Cluster Mode enabled, configuring multiple shards, each with a primary and at least one read replica across different Availability Zones, with Multi-AZ automatic failover enabled so a replica is promoted automatically if a shard's primary fails. B. Use ElastiCache for Memcached with multiple nodes, since Memcached natively supports both automatic failover and data sharding. C. Use a single large ElastiCache for Redis node with Cluster Mode disabled and no replicas, and vertically scale it whenever more throughput is needed. D. Use ElastiCache for Redis with Cluster Mode disabled, manually add read replicas without Multi-AZ, and perform manual failover via the console if the primary fails. Redis Cluster Mode enabled is the only configuration described that provides both requirements simultaneously: sharding data across multiple node groups for horizontal scaling of throughput, and Multi-AZ automatic failover within each shard, promoting a replica to primary automatically -- the standard, purpose-built answer for a scalable, highly available Redis deployment. B is wrong because Memcached has no native replication, no automatic failover, and no built-in high availability at all; a node failure loses that node's data entirely. C is wrong because a single node with no replicas has no automatic failover target, and vertical scaling has ceiling limits and requires downtime, unlike horizontal shard scaling. D is wrong because this configuration explicitly disables Multi-AZ and specifies manual failover, failing the automatic-failover requirement, and Cluster Mode disabled does not shard data across multiple node groups. question: A Lambda-based serverless application experiences connection exhaustion errors against its Aurora MySQL database during traffic spikes, because each concurrent Lambda invocation opens its own new database connection, and Aurora failover events cause a spike of application connection errors that take too long to recover from.

options.A: Increase the Aurora instance's max_connections parameter to the highest possible value to accommodate more simultaneous Lambda connections.
options.B: Introduce Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora cluster; Lambda functions connect to the RDS Proxy endpoint instead of directly to the database, and RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes connections, reducing total connections against the database, while also reducing application-visible failover time by maintaining the pool and quickly switching to the new writer.
options.C: Switch the application from Lambda to a fleet of always-on EC2 instances, since EC2 instances inherently manage database connections more efficiently than Lambda.
options.D: Reduce Lambda's reserved concurrency to 1 so that only one database connection is ever open at a time. Design High-Performing Architectures AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 19

B. ✓ Introduce Amazon RDS Proxy in front of the Aurora cluster; Lambda functions connect to the RDS Proxy endpoint instead of directly to the database, and RDS Proxy pools and multiplexes connections, reducing total connections against the database, while also reducing application-visible failover time by maintaining the pool and quickly switching to the new writer. C. Switch the application from Lambda to a fleet of always-on EC2 instances, since EC2 instances inherently manage database connections more efficiently than Lambda. D. Reduce Lambda's reserved concurrency to 1 so that only one database connection is ever open at a time. RDS Proxy is specifically designed to solve this exact serverless connection-management problem: it sits between the application and the database, pooling and multiplexing many client connections into a much smaller number of actual database connections, preventing connection exhaustion, and significantly reducing application-visible failover time by maintaining the pool and rerouting to the new writer quickly. A is wrong because raising max_connections has a hard ceiling based on instance memory, does not address the underlying inefficiency of a connection-per-invocation pattern, and does not help with failover speed. C is wrong because this is a major, unnecessary architectural change, and "EC2 inherently manages connections better" is not accurate on its own; connection pooling, not the compute platform, is the actual fix. D is wrong because throttling concurrency to 1 eliminates the application's ability to handle concurrent traffic at all, severely degrading performance during exactly the traffic spikes the design must handle. question: An ECS Fargate service processes messages from an SQS queue. During traffic spikes, the queue backs up significantly because the number of running tasks does not increase quickly enough, even though CPU and memory utilization of existing tasks stays moderate. The team wants task count to scale directly based on the queue backlog.

options.A: Configure ECS Service Auto Scaling using target tracking on the ECSServiceAverageCPUUtilization metric only, since CPU is the standard metric for all ECS scaling scenarios.
options.B: Manually monitor the SQS queue depth via CloudWatch dashboards and manually update the ECS service's desired count using the console during business hours.
options.C: Configure Application Auto Scaling for the ECS service using a target tracking or step scaling policy based on the CloudWatch metric ApproximateNumberOfMessagesVisible, often normalized as backlog per task, so task count scales in direct response to queue depth rather than an indirect CPU signal.
options.D: Enable Fargate Spot exclusively, since Spot capacity automatically scales based on any CloudWatch metric without configuration.

question: A team runs large, complex analytical SELECT queries with full table scans against a very large Aurora MySQL table, hundreds of GB in size, for reporting, and query performance is bottlenecked by the amount of data that must be pulled from storage into the database instance's compute layer for processing.

options.A: Increase the Aurora MySQL writer instance size to the largest available instance class to add more CPU and memory for query processing.
options.B: Add more Aurora Replicas and manually shard the large table's rows evenly across them.
options.C: Migrate the reporting workload to run directly against the Multi-AZ standby instance, since standby instances offer dedicated compute for read-only analytical queries.
options.D: Enable Aurora Parallel Query, which pushes portions of query processing, such as filtering and aggregation, down into the distributed storage layer itself, parallelizing work across storage nodes and reducing the amount of data transferred to the database instance for large analytical scans. question: (Select TWO) A SaaS company has dozens of small-to-medium customer databases with highly unpredictable, spiky usage patterns -- some customers are idle for hours then suddenly generate heavy load -- and provisioning fixed-capacity Aurora instances per customer is wasting money during idle periods while occasionally under-provisioning during spikes. Which TWO characteristics make Aurora Serverless v2 well suited to this requirement?

options.A: Aurora Serverless v2 scales compute capacity, in fine-grained ACU increments, automatically and near-instantaneously in response to load, without requiring a database restart or connection disruption, addressing both the idle-cost-waste and spike-under-provisioning problems.
options.B: Aurora Serverless v2 guarantees zero cost during idle periods because it fully pauses to zero capacity and stops billing entirely whenever there are no active connections.
options.C: Aurora Serverless v2 can be used as a reader or writer within a standard Aurora cluster, including mixed with provisioned instances, and integrates with familiar Aurora features such as Global Database and Aurora Replicas, simplifying adoption across the company's many databases.
options.D: Aurora Serverless v2 eliminates the need for any database engine, since it runs entirely on a proprietary in-memory engine unrelated to MySQL or PostgreSQL.
options.E: Aurora Serverless v2 requires manually triggering a scaling event via an API call whenever load changes, since it does not support automatic scaling.

question: A read-heavy product catalog application uses ElastiCache for Redis as a cache in front of a relational database. The team notices that immediately after a cache node restarts and loses its cached data, the database experiences a huge spike in load as many requests simultaneously miss the cache and query the database directly, sometimes causing a cascading failure. What caching strategy consideration would BEST address this specific thundering-herd problem?

options.A: Switch entirely from lazy loading, or cache-aside, to a write-through caching strategy, since write-through eliminates all cache misses permanently.
options.B: Keep lazy loading as the primary strategy, but add jittered or staggered TTL expiration values rather than identical TTLs, and add a short-lived mutex or request coalescing so that only one request per key fetches from the database on a miss while others wait for the resulting cached value, reducing simultaneous duplicate database hits after a cold cache or expiration spike.
options.C: Set all cached items to have no TTL so that a cache restart never causes any misses.
options.D: Increase the size of the ElastiCache node so it can never restart or fail.

explanation: A read-heavy product catalog application uses ElastiCache for Redis as a cache in front of a relational database. The team notices that immediately after a cache node restarts and loses its cached data, the database experiences a huge spike in load as many requests simultaneously miss the cache and query the database directly, sometimes causing a cascading failure. What caching strategy consideration would BEST address this specific thundering-herd problem? A. Switch entirely from lazy loading, or cache-aside, to a write-through caching strategy, since write-through eliminates all cache misses permanently. B. ✓ Keep lazy loading as the primary strategy, but add jittered or staggered TTL expiration values rather than identical TTLs, and add a short-lived mutex or request coalescing so that only one request per key fetches from the database on a miss while others wait for the resulting cached value, reducing simultaneous duplicate database hits after a cold cache or expiration spike. C. Set all cached items to have no TTL so that a cache restart never causes any misses. D. Increase the size of the ElastiCache node so it can never restart or fail. The thundering-herd or cache-stampede problem, where many simultaneous requests miss the cache and hammer the database at once, is best mitigated within a lazy-loading strategy by staggering TTLs so keys do not all expire simultaneously, and by using request coalescing or a short lock so only one request repopulates a given key from the database while concurrent requests wait for that result -- directly targeting the "many simultaneous misses" root cause. A is wrong because write-through does not eliminate cache misses for a cold or restarted cache, which remains empty until items are written again, and adds write-path latency for every write regardless of whether that data is ever read. C is risky because never expiring cached items causes stale-data problems and does not address the actual triggering event, since a restart still empties the cache regardless of TTL settings. D is wrong because no cache node can be guaranteed to never restart or fail, so this does not reliably prevent the scenario or address the underlying stampede problem when a restart does occur. question: A high-traffic application performs the same DynamoDB lookups repeatedly for popular items, such as trending product details, and needs to reduce response times from single-digit milliseconds down to microseconds for these read-heavy, repeat-read patterns, without re-architecting the application's core data model or adding a separate general-purpose caching cluster to manage.

options.A: Enable DynamoDB Streams and process every read request through a Lambda function backed by ElastiCache for additional caching.
options.B: Switch the table's capacity mode from provisioned to on-demand, since on-demand capacity mode inherently provides microsecond read latency.
options.C: Enable DynamoDB Accelerator, or DAX, an in-memory, DynamoDB-API-compatible caching layer that sits in front of DynamoDB, requiring only pointing the SDK client to the DAX cluster endpoint, and reducing read latency from milliseconds to microseconds for cached items.
options.D: Increase the table's provisioned Read Capacity Units substantially, since higher RCU always results in proportionally lower per-request latency. AWS Certified Solutions Architect - Associate (SAA-C03) Practice Exam Page 22

question: (Select TWO) A DynamoDB table using a partition key of OrderDate, for example "2026-08-09", experiences severe throttling during peak traffic, even though the table's overall aggregate provisioned throughput is well above the total request rate, because the vast majority of requests target the current date's partition key value while older dates receive almost no traffic. Which TWO changes would best resolve this hot-partition problem?

options.A: Redesign the partition key to include higher-cardinality, more evenly distributed data, for example a composite key combining OrderDate with a random suffix or a high-cardinality attribute like OrderID or CustomerID, so write and read traffic spreads across many distinct partition key values instead of concentrating on a single value per day.
options.B: Switch the table to on-demand capacity mode, which by itself guarantees no partition will ever be throttled, regardless of partition key design.
options.C: Enable DynamoDB auto scaling for provisioned capacity, since auto scaling automatically redistributes an individual hot partition's traffic across all other partitions in the table.
options.D: Simply increase the total provisioned RCU and WCU for the table substantially, without changing the partition key design, understanding that DynamoDB divides throughput relatively evenly across partitions, so a poorly distributed key can still cause a single partition to be throttled even when aggregate table capacity is high.
options.E: Consider DynamoDB's adaptive capacity, which works automatically in the background to accommodate imbalanced access patterns to some degree, as a complementary safety net while primarily fixing the root cause via better key design, since adaptive capacity alone cannot fully compensate for a severely skewed access pattern concentrated on a single key value.

question: A company runs a real-time multiplayer gaming backend using a custom TCP-based protocol, not HTTP or HTTPS, hosted on EC2 behind Network Load Balancers across multiple AWS Regions, and needs to route players to the optimal, lowest-latency healthy regional endpoint using static anycast IP addresses, with fast failover if a region becomes unhealthy.

question: A company generates application log files written to S3 continuously. Logs are accessed frequently during the first 30 days for troubleshooting, rarely accessed between day 30 and day 90, and almost never accessed after day 90 but must be retained for 5 years for compliance, after which they should be automatically deleted. Design the most cost-effective S3 lifecycle configuration.

options.A: Store all logs in S3 Standard for the full 5-year retention period, then manually delete them after 5 years, since S3 Standard provides the best balance of cost and accessibility for compliance data.
options.B: Use S3 Intelligent-Tiering exclusively with no lifecycle expiration rule, relying on its automatic tiering alone to eventually reduce storage costs to near zero after 5 years.
options.C: Store all logs directly in S3 Glacier Deep Archive from day one, since it has the lowest storage cost and logs are compliance data that does not need frequent access.
options.D: Configure an S3 Lifecycle policy that transitions objects from S3 Standard to S3 Standard-IA at 30 days, transitions to S3 Glacier Flexible Retrieval or Deep Archive at 90 days, and adds an expiration action to permanently delete objects after 5 years, or 1,825 days.
